title: Conifer well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Around Conifer, the median well depth is 302 ft and typical finished residential wells run about $25,600-$42,200 based on recent drilling data.
h1: Well depths, yields, and drilling costs around Conifer
intro_html:
In the Conifer area, wells are going into fractured mountain bedrock, not big sand aquifers. That means depth and yield jump around a bit from lot to lot. Looking at a 5‑mile radius around town gives a good picture of what you’re likely to hit on a new build or a replacement well.

Below is what the Colorado DWR records show for well depths, production, water levels, drilling activity, and typical cost so you can budget and judge a property with eyes open.

sections.heading: How deep wells run around Conifer
sections.html:
Within about 5 miles of Conifer, the median well depth is 302 feet. The middle half of wells runs from 190 to 480 feet, so most bids will be built around that kind of range, with contingencies if the hole has to go deeper. About 36% of wells are between 100 and 300 feet, and 40% land between 300 and 600 feet. Another 15% go past 600 feet, and the deepest well on record reaches 1,703 feet, which shows how unpredictable fractured bedrock can be.

For budgeting and planning, assume you could land near that 302‑foot median, but recognize you might easily end up in the 400–600 foot group, especially on higher ridges or rocky knobs between Conifer and Aspen Park or up toward Brook Forest.

sections.heading: Well yield and how much water you get
sections.html:
Production in this area is decent for mountain fractured rock. The median reported yield is 5.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half of wells between 2.6 and 8.0 gpm. Only about 4% of wells report under 1 gpm, which is the “problem well” category, while 39% fall between 1 and 5 gpm and 51% are in the 5 to 15 gpm range. About 6% exceed 15 gpm.

For a typical exempt household-use permit, anything above about 2–3 gpm with some storage usually works fine. Still, that 4% under 1 gpm matters: on rocky sites between Conifer and Pine or up toward Indian Hills, you want to check neighboring well yields carefully before committing to a build.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they’re doing over time
sections.html:
Where static water levels are reported, the median depth to water is 73 feet, with the middle half between 35 and 160 feet below ground. That’s the distance from the surface down to the standing water in the well, not the bottom of the hole. Historically, the median static level was around 41 to 57 feet in the 1960s and 1970s, then about 42 feet in the 1980s.

In the 1990s, the median jumped to about 150 feet, then improved somewhat to 120 feet in the 2000s and 91 feet in the 2010s, with the 2020s around 100 feet. Overall, that suggests the water table is deeper now than in the 1960s–1980s, so pumps and power sizing around Conifer, Evergreen, and Upper Bear Creek need to account for a fairly deep lift.

sections.heading: Who has been drilling wells here and when
sections.html:
There are 9,516 well permits in the records in this part of Jefferson County, with 6,416 listed as constructed and 6,566 reporting a total depth. Drilling really took off in the 1970s, with 2,656 permits that decade, then 1,506 in the 1980s and 1,917 in the 1990s. Activity tapered to 867 permits in the 2000s, 396 in the 2010s, and 254 so far in the 2020s, with the newest permit showing up in 2025.

Most wells are for domestic or household use, about 93%, with small shares for stock and monitoring. The work is almost entirely in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, with a few Fractured Crystalline and Alluvial wells. Around Conifer, Aspen Park, and toward Pine, the most active drillers on record are Living Water Systems Inc. (Robert Goble), Aspen Drilling Company Inc (Leroy J. Beery), and Walton.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Conifer
sections.html:
Here the bit is chewing through fractured granite and gneiss, so drilling is slower and pricier than on the plains. Typical drilling rates run about $65 to $100 per foot. At the 302‑foot median depth, that puts the bare drilled hole roughly in the $19,600 to $30,200 range.

By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished residential well around Conifer usually pencils out around $25,600 to $42,200 at that median depth. If you end up in the 480‑foot middle-upper range or into the 600+ foot group, total cost climbs fast, so it’s smart to have a budget buffer rather than bidding to the optimistic side.

sections.heading: Local risks: low yield, contamination, and siting
sections.html:
In fractured bedrock, the main risk is a low-yield or marginal well. With 4% of reported wells under 1 gpm, that’s not common, but it’s real. A few wells also end up very deep compared to neighbors. Good siting, using nearby well logs and topography, matters a lot on ridges around Conifer, Indian Hills, and Evergreen.

On the water-quality side, within about 10 miles there are 17 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 33 historic mine features, and 51 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That doesn’t mean your water is bad, but it does mean you should test a new or existing well for a full panel, including metals and PFAS, and be careful with well–septic separation and drainfield placement on tight lots.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Conifer well lot
sections.html:
For a vacant lot, first thing I’d pull are nearby well permits within a mile or so to see typical depths and yields. Around Conifer and Aspen Park, a 190 to 480 foot range and 2.6 to 8.0 gpm middle‑half yield is common, but you’ll want to know if your spot sits among the deeper or weaker producers.

Confirm that the permit allows the use you need: most here are exempt domestic/household wells, which come with limits and can’t cover big irrigation. Check static water level and pump depth on existing wells, and budget realistically using the 302‑foot median and the cost ranges above. Finally, line up well, septic, and building envelopes so setbacks, drive access, and drill rig access all work before you close on a property.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Conifer, Colorado?
faq.a: In the Conifer area, the median well depth is 302 feet. The middle half of wells lies between 190 and 480 feet, with about 36% in the 100–300 foot range and 40% between 300 and 600 feet. Around 15% of wells go deeper than 600 feet, and a few extreme cases run much deeper, so drilling bids usually include a depth allowance above the minimum estimate.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Conifer?
faq.a: In fractured mountain bedrock around Conifer, typical drilling rates are about $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 302 feet, that puts the bare hole roughly at $19,600 to $30,200. A complete residential setup with casing, pump, tank, trenching, and electrical usually ends up around $25,600 to $42,200 at that depth, with costs rising if your well needs to go significantly deeper.

faq.q: What is a good well yield in Conifer, Colorado?
faq.a: Wells around Conifer show a median yield of 5.0 gpm, with the middle half between 2.6 and 8.0 gpm. About 51% of wells fall in the 5–15 gpm range, which is solid production for a single home on an exempt well. Only about 4% of wells report under 1 gpm, but that low-yield group is why it’s important to review nearby well logs before buying or designing a new build.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in the Conifer area?
faq.a: Water quality varies by location and construction. Within roughly 10 miles of Conifer there are 17 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 33 historic mine features, and 51 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those are regional flags, not automatic problems, but they are strong reasons to lab-test any well for bacteria, metals, and PFAS, and to keep septic systems properly sited and maintained uphill of the well.

faq.q: Are water tables dropping around Conifer, Colorado?
faq.a: Static water level records show shallower median depths of about 41 to 57 feet in the 1960s and 1970s, and about 42 feet in the 1980s. By the 1990s the median jumped to around 150 feet, then improved somewhat to 120 feet in the 2000s and 91 feet in the 2010s, with about 100 feet in the 2020s. That pattern suggests water levels here are generally deeper now than in the earlier decades.
